sibling_pages_structure.title: Simple Wedding Ceremony Script With Legal Lines Marked
sibling_pages_structure.structure: Five parts with timings (before guests sit, welcome and story, the legal lines, own vows and rings, pronouncement and signing), about 12 minutes. Sections on legal lines for Australia, England and Wales, New York and a symbolic ceremony anywhere; lines to adjust for families; timing; what you can cut; hand the script over; when something goes wrong; FAQ.
sibling_pages_structure.do_not_duplicate: Multi-country legal lines block, family-adjustment lines, 12-minute guest ceremony, cut list. Link with a non-exact anchor such as 'a short ceremony with guests'.

sibling_pages_structure.title: Humorous Wedding Ceremony Script With Full Wording
sibling_pages_structure.structure: Where jokes work; full script (processional, welcome, how you met, a few words on marriage, declaration, smaller promises, vows, rings, pronouncement and kiss, recessional); gentler and bolder joke swaps; a ceremony abroad after signing at home; length 6 to 8 minutes; delivery; FAQ. Legal examples cite California Family Code s 420 and New York s 12.
sibling_pages_structure.do_not_duplicate: Joke swaps, 'smaller promises' section, processional and recessional for guests, US legal lines. Our elopement script should have no processional, no guest address, and speak to two people plus celebrant and witnesses.

sibling_pages_structure.title: Elopement Vows and How to Write Them for Two
sibling_pages_structure.structure: What makes elopement vows different; five-step writing guide; four example vows (short, traditional, adventurous, quiet); where and when to exchange vows; private or witnessed vows; recording; sharing the news; planning with Wedded Wonderland; FAQ.
sibling_pages_structure.do_not_duplicate: Vow writing steps and the four example vows. Link for vows instead of writing a vow guide; script should leave a [your vows] slot.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2): 'Where a marriage is solemnised by an authorised celebrant, not being a minister of religion, it is sufficient if each of the parties says to the other, in the presence of the authorised celebrant and the witnesses, the words: "I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)"; or words to that effect.'
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Quote exactly in the script as the legal vow line. Each partner says it to the other. Deciding authority: the authorised celebrant, under AGD.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(1): where the authorised celebrant is a minister of religion, the marriage 'may be solemnised according to any form and ceremony recognised as sufficient for the purpose by the religious body or organisation of which he or she is a minister.'
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: One line: a religious elopement follows the minister's rite, so the template is for civil celebrants.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 46(1) (the monitum): where the authorised celebrant is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination, the celebrant 'shall say to the parties, in the presence of the witnesses, the words: "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law. Before you are joined in marriage in my presence and in the presence of these witnesses, I am to remind you of the solemn and binding nature of the relationship into which you are now about to enter. Marriage, according to law in Australia, is the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life."; or words to that effect.'
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Said by the celebrant, not the couple, before the vows. Quote exactly in the script.

facts.claim: Section 44 of the Marriage Act 1961: a marriage shall not be solemnised unless at least 2 persons who are, or appear to the person solemnising the marriage to be, over the age of 18 years are present as witnesses.
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation 9 July 2024)
facts.use_note: An elopement for two in Australia still needs two adult witnesses. Corroborated live on AGD 2026-11-22 ('Witnesses must be over 18 years old').

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: 'A celebrant must be physically present to solemnise a marriage, together with the parties and 2 witnesses.' On the day, 3 marriage certificates are signed by the couple, the celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18; the celebrant lodges the paperwork with the state or territory registry of births, deaths and marriages within 14 days.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Minimum people at a legal Australian elopement: the couple, an authorised celebrant and 2 witnesses, all physically present. No video-link ceremony. Whether the celebrant can double as a witness is not sourced (N-02); write 'two people besides your celebrant'.

facts.claim: To marry in Australia you must, among other things: be at least 18; understand what marriage means and freely agree to marry; use specific words during the ceremony; give a NOIM to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding; and be married by an authorised marriage celebrant. You do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Short checklist for the 'is it legal' section. NOIM timing re-read live 2026-11-22, unchanged.

facts.claim: The NOIM must be completed, signed and given to an authorised celebrant at least one month, and not more than 18 months, before the proposed marriage, unless a prescribed authority has agreed to shorten the notice period (section 42 of the Act).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Spontaneous elopements in Australia still need a month's notice. Say 'given no more than 18 months before', not 'valid for 18 months'.

facts.claim: If there is less than one month until the wedding, the couple should talk to their celebrant; they may be able to marry if a prescribed authority approves shortening the notice period. AGD lists these reasons: employment-related or travel commitments; wedding or celebration arrangements; medical reasons; legal proceedings; error in giving notice.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Do not imply approval is automatic. Say 'the official your celebrant can point you to'.

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM may be witnessed in person or remotely by audio-visual link. If the couple is in Australia, the remote witness (which can be a celebrant) must also be in Australia; if the couple is outside Australia, the authorised witness (who cannot be a celebrant) must also be outside Australia. AGD confirms you can complete the NOIM while overseas if you plan to marry in Australia.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage
facts.use_note: Remote witnessing applies to the NOIM only, never the ceremony (F-05).

facts.claim: Changes that became law on 12 June 2024 include that the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before solemnising the marriage.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Build a short pre-ceremony moment into the plan: the celebrant meets each of you separately.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2) wording ends 'or words to that effect', and s 46(1) likewise. Nothing in s 45 or s 46 bars couples from adding their own vows; the Act sets the minimum words that must be said.
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961
facts.use_note: Second sentence is our reading of the statute. Phrase as: 'your own vows go alongside the legal words, and your celebrant confirms the final wording'.

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: 'Overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant and cannot be registered in Australia. An overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was a valid marriage in the overseas country and would have been a valid marriage here.'
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Get married
facts.use_note: Core of the 'abroad' section: an Australian celebrant reading this script overseas makes it symbolic. The legal step is done at home or under local law.

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), Getting married overseas
facts.use_note: Second official source alongside F-12. Local legal rules in each destination are not covered here (N-04).

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines 11.6 and 11.7: celebrants may conduct commitment ceremonies, which are not marriages and must not purport to be one. The celebrant must not prepare or submit any paperwork (such as the NOIM). Witnesses are not required for a commitment ceremony. A certificate of marriage, or any certificate referring to the Marriage Act, must not be prepared, and celebrants should avoid the words 'wedding' or 'marriage'.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (version 4.0, July 2018)
facts.use_note: Supports 'a symbolic elopement needs no witnesses and can use any words'. Medium: 2018 edition; the September 2021 edition not opened (N-03).

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines (Part 5.8): arranging witnesses is the couple's responsibility; the celebrant is not responsible for providing them. It is best practice (but not a requirement of the Marriage Act) that the witnesses know the parties.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for authorised celebrants (version 4.0, July 2018)
facts.use_note: Elopement tip: decide your two witnesses early (a photographer or planner can legally serve, but best practice is people who know you). Do not say the celebrant will supply them.

facts.claim: There are four types of authorised marriage celebrant (Commonwealth-registered marriage celebrants, Commonwealth-registered religious marriage celebrants, ministers of religion of a recognised denomination, and state and territory officers). AGD keeps a searchable database of all authorised celebrants at marriage.ag.gov.au.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Find a marriage celebrant
facts.use_note: Tip: check your celebrant on the AGD register before you book.

facts.claim: Our Simple Wedding Ceremony Script runs in five parts (welcome, your story, the legal words, your vows and rings, the walk back), reads aloud in about 12 minutes, and says only the legal lines are fixed and whoever conducts the legal part confirms them. It includes legal lines for Australia, England and Wales, New York and a symbolic ceremony anywhere.
facts.publisher: Wedded Wonderland
facts.use_note: Sibling page. Link, do not repeat its multi-country legal block or 12-minute guest structure.

facts.claim: Our Humorous Wedding Ceremony Script says jokes can go anywhere except the legal declaration, the written script is about 500 words, and the ceremony runs 6 to 8 minutes with personal vows. It has a section on a ceremony abroad after signing at home.
facts.publisher: Wedded Wonderland
facts.use_note: Length figures from a Firecrawl summary of the page, not a direct quote; confirm before citing numbers. Link for a playful tone.

facts.claim: Our Elopement Vows guide: elopement vows are personal promises made in a private ceremony, spoken to one person and no one else; 'One to two minutes each, or about 150 to 250 words, suits a spoken exchange.' It notes many countries require witnesses for a legal marriage and some allow a private exchange alongside it.
facts.publisher: Wedded Wonderland
facts.use_note: House line on elopement vow length. Link for the vows slot in the script.

facts.claim: Our What Is an Elopement page: 'An elopement is a small wedding planned around the two of you, usually with fewer than 20 guests and sometimes none at all.' 'If you are eloping in Australia, you need two adult witnesses for the marriage to be legal, even with no other guests.' 'Many couples keep the ceremony abroad symbolic and sign the paperwork at a registry at home before or after they travel.'
facts.publisher: Wedded Wonderland
facts.use_note: Consistent with F-04 and F-12. Internal link for 'what an elopement is'.

facts.claim: Our Is Eloping Legal page says couples can't solemnise their own marriage in Australia, and suggests 'a quick legal ceremony before you leave, with the vows and celebration overseas.'
facts.publisher: Wedded Wonderland
facts.use_note: Internal link for the legal detail so this article stays a script. Self-solemnising is consistent with F-05 and F-06 (an authorised celebrant must solemnise).

legal.summary: s 45(2) legal vow words, said by each party in the presence of the celebrant and witnesses, or words to that effect. Confirmed by the authorised celebrant under AGD.
s 45(1) ministers of religion use their religious body's form.
s 46(1) monitum said by the civil celebrant in the presence of the witnesses.
s 44 at least 2 witnesses over 18. Confirmed by AGD.
Celebrant, couple and 2 witnesses physically present; 3 certificates signed; lodged with BDM within 14 days. Confirmed by AGD.
Eligibility, specific words, NOIM, authorised celebrant. Confirmed by AGD.
NOIM at least 1 month and not more than 18 months before, unless shortened by a prescribed authority. Confirmed by AGD.
Shortening of time grounds; talk to your celebrant. Confirmed by AGD.
Remote NOIM witnessing; NOIM can be completed overseas. Confirmed by AGD.
Celebrant meets each party separately in person before the marriage. Confirmed by AGD.
Act sets minimum words; personal vows sit alongside (our reading, medium). Celebrant confirms.
Australian celebrants cannot perform overseas marriages; overseas marriages generally recognised. Confirmed by AGD.
Overseas marriages not registrable but generally recognised. Confirmed by Smartraveller (DFAT).
Commitment (symbolic) ceremonies are not marriages; no NOIM, no certificate, no witnesses required. AGD Guidelines (2018).
Couple arranges witnesses; knowing them is best practice. AGD Guidelines (2018).
Four celebrant types; AGD register at marriage.ag.gov.au.
